a b s t r a c t
Electrochemical reduction of CO2 in an aqueous 0.5 M KHCO3 solution is studied by use of novel nanostructured CueAu alloys, which are prepared through electrochemical deposition with a nanoporous Cu film (NCF) as template. Linear voltammetry results show that the as-synthesized CueAu alloys exhibit obvious catalysis towards electrochemical reduction of CO2. Further analysis of products reveals that faradic efficiencies of alcohols (methanol and ethanol) are greatly dependent on the nanostructures and compositions of CueAu alloys. It is expected that this work could provide new insight into the development of powerful electrocatalysts for reduction of CO2 to alcohols.

sections.heading: 1. Introduction
sections.text:
Direct electrochemical reduction of CO2 has attracted much attention over recent decades as this offers a convenient route to convertwaste CO2 into useful organics [1,2]. In addition, this process provides a potential solution for the storage of energy in chemical fuels for energy sources. For example, electricity from renewable solar power could be stored in chemical form via electrochemical reduction of CO2 [3]. And the reduction products can be sources for
All rights reserved.
automobile fuels or generation of electricity again by fuel cells. Amongst various possible products of CO2 reduction in aqueous system, alcohols such as methanol and ethanol are desirable owing to their high energy density and easy transportation. However, the conversion efficiencies of CO2 to alcohols on metal-based catalysts are still very low by present. To improve the conversion efficiency of CO2 to alcohols, it is essential to develop new electrocatalysts.
Hori et al. have demonstrated that the product selectivity during CO2 reduction is in fact very sensitive to the electro-catalysts used [1]. Among pure metallic electrodes, only copper electrode is demonstrated to be able to catalyze the conversion of CO2 to alcohols [4]. Unfortunately, faradic efficiencies of alcohols are
relatively low (less than 1% for methanol) and major products are CO, formate and hydrocarbons [5]. A recent report showed that Cu2O electrode could catalyze the conversion of CO2 to methanol with a high faradaic efficiency of 38% [6]. However, the Cu2O tended to be reduced and lost catalytic function. In comparison, considerable progress has been achieved on the conversion of CO2 to CO with faradic efficiency up to 96% [7]. The reason could be that CO is initially produced before the formation of alcohols at more negative potentials. Although the formation mechanism of alcohols is not clear in detail, it is widely accepted that CO2 is initially reduced to CO, which is further converted to alcohols or other hydrocarbons. Considering that the reduction of CO2 to alcohols goes through multistep electron-transfer pathways, sole Cu metal may not be

capable of catalyzing the conversion of CO2 to alcohols efficiently. Therefore, Cu alloys were tried in the electrochemical reduction of CO2 and showed distinct behaviors from those of pure metals [8]. These results indicated that development of new electrocatalysts based on the composites of Cu and other metals could be a possible way to improve the yield of alcohols.
In this article, nanostructured CueAu alloys were synthesized for electrochemical reduction of CO2 in aqueous solution for the first time. To ensure clean surface of catalysts, no organic additives were used and nanostructured CueAu alloys were obtained by electrochemical deposition with a nanoporous Cu film (NCF) as template. While it is possible to vary film morphology and structure, in this communication we examine only the effect of varying the alloy composition on conversion efficiency of CO2 to alcohols, demonstrating encouraging results for these novel catalysts.

sections.heading: 2. Experimental
sections.text:
2.1. Fabrication of nanostructured CueAu alloys for electrocatalytic reduction of CO2
NCF/Cu electrodewas prepared by a similar process published in our previous work [10]. In brief, NCF/Cu electrodewas fabricated by electrochemical dealloying of thermal-treated CueZn sample in 25mMHCl using linear sweep voltammetry (LSV).With the NCF/Cu electrode as working electrode (2 cm2 exposed area), electrodeposition of nanostructured CueAu alloy was conducted under constant potential in solution containing 0.1 MH2SO4, 5mMCuSO4, and 5 mM HAuCl4. A saturated calomel electrode (SCE) and a platinum plate were used as reference electrode and counter electrode, respectively. The total deposition charge was set to 0.2 C. The as-synthesized CueAu alloy electrodes were then used as working electrode and immersed into electrolyte with 2 cm2 exposed area. The electrochemical behaviors of CueAu alloy electrodes were evaluated by LSV in a phosphate buffered solution (PBS, 0.2 M Na2SO4, 0.2 M NaH2PO4eNa2HPO4, pH 7.6) saturated with either CO2 or Ar. Bulk electro-reduction of CO2 was performed in an H-type cell separated by a cation exchangemembrane (Nafion 117). Before this electrolysis, a catholyte of 0.5 M KHCO3 solution was bubbled with Ar to remove oxygen and then saturated with ultrapure CO2 (99.999%) by bubbling for 30 min (298 K, pH 7.6). Bulk electrolysis was carried out at 1.1 V (vs. SCE) and total
consumed charge was 8 C per sample. For the test of Cu or Au nanoparticles, 8 mg powder of Cu nanoparticles (20e40 nm, Alfa Aesar) or Au nanoparticles (20e25 nm, Alfa Aesar) were ultrasonically dispersed in 1 mL Nafion solution (0.5 wt%) and 0.25 mL of mixture was dropped onto a carbon cloth (2 cm2 area, Japan, NOKH2315 GDL) as nanostructured electrode. These were then dried in a vacuum-oven at 50 C for 2 h to remove residual alcohols of Nafion solution.

sections.heading: 2.2. Characterization and analysis of products
sections.text:
Themorphologies of samples were observed using a JEOL-6700F field emission scanning electron microscopy (FESEM). X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns were recorded on a Philips MPD 18801 diffraction-meter (CuKa radiation, l¼ 1.5418 A, 20 kV,150mA). The surface compositions of CueAu deposits were analyzed through Xray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) on a spectrometer (VG Scientific ESCALAB Mark II, Al anode). The concentrations of methanol and ethanol produced in solution by the electrochemical reduction of CO2 were analyzed using a gas chromatograph (GC, Hengxin GC2020) equipped with FID detector and capillary column (PEG-20M). To avoid damage to the GC caused by the presence of salt in the
solutions, the electrolyte was mixed with Amberlite IRN-150 ionexchange resin (Alfa Aesar) and filtered to remove KHCO3 before GC analysis [11]. The temperatures of injector and detector were both held at 200 C. After injection of 1 mL solution sample, the oven temperature was held at 40 C for the first 4 min, which was optimum for the separation of methanol and ethanol components. Then the oven temperature was increased to 120 C at 20 C min 1 to remove the water from GC completely. The concentration of formate in liquid products was analyzed by an ion chromatograph (ICS-900, Dionex Corporation).

sections.heading: 3. Results and discussion
sections.text:
Determination of a suitable solution is the first step to fabricate nanostructured CueAu alloys on NCF/Cu. Fig. 1a shows the reduction behavior of Cu2þ and AuCl4
on the surface of Cu electrode. In a solution of 5 mM CuSO4, the strong reduction peak at 0.68 V is associated with bulk deposition of Cu (0) (black line) while the weak peak at 0.22 V results from the reduction of Cu(II) to Cu(I). As for the solution containing 5 mM HAuCl4, the cathodic peak at 0.03 V is ascribed to the deposition of Au(0) (red line). When both CuSO4 and HAuCl4 are present in solution, the characteristic peak corresponding to the deposition of Cu disappears and a new cathodic peak appears at 0.16 V (blue line), which is probably attributed to the co-reduction of Cu2þ and AuCl4
into CueAu alloy (For interpretation of the references to color in this paragraph, the reader is referred to the web version of this article.).
A similar electrochemical technique was used to deposit CueAu onto NCF electrode at 0.26 V and XPS analysis indicates its composition to be Cu63.9Au36.1. XRD results for this CueAu deposit plus a pure Au deposit (from 5 mM HAuCl4 at the same potential) are shown in Fig. 1b. The diffraction peaks of Cu resulted from that of porous copper film. As for pure Au deposited on NCF, diffraction peaks at 38.2, 44.5, 64.8 and 77.6 can be ascribed to Au (111), (200), (220) and (311) reflections, respectively. Different from that of pure
Au, the diffraction peaks of CueAu samples shift to higher diffraction angles, indicating that the deposit is composed of CueAu alloy. Fig. 1c and d shows SEM images depicting the morphology of the original NCF and that after deposition of the CueAu film, respectively. The original NCF is a kind of 3D nanostructured networkwith ligaments of approximately 40 nm in size (Fig. 1c). After deposition of CueAu alloy, the ligament size of NCF increases to w70 nm but the 3D nanostructured networks remain (Fig. 1d), indicating that CueAu is mostly deposited on the surface of ligaments. It can be seen that the surface of ligaments is not smooth and there are very fine nanoparticles (less than w20 nm) on the surface. However, CueAu nanoparticles deposited on a smooth copper substrate are much bigger (w70 nm, Fig. 1e), indicating that the porous structure of NCF has a great effect on the morphology of deposited Cu-Au nanoparticles.
Electrochemical reduction of CO2 was investigated on different Cu electrodes and results are shown in Fig. 2. Using Cu63.9Au36.1/ NCF electrode, hydrogen evolution occurs at about 1.1 V in the Ar bubbled solution (Fig. 2a). In presence of CO2, the cathodic current increases at potential more negative than 1.0 V, indicating that participation of CO2 reduction contributes to the enhancement of cathodic current. In comparison, hydrogen evolution starts at 1.0 V and the current is slightly suppressed by CO2 reduction on nanostructured Cu electrode (Fig. 2b). Such suppression occurs owing to presence of adsorbed species generated during CO2 reduction [12]. The difference in electrochemical behaviors indicates that the nanostructured CueAu alloy may favor conversion of CO2 and its intermediate species, which leads to the increase of current in presence of CO2. However, only currentepotential relationships are not enough to judge if thesematerials could catalyze conversion of CO2 into alcohols. It is necessary to quantitatively analyze the products after bulk electrolysis of CO2.
The presence of alcohols in liquid products is confirmed through GC analysis, and the peaks correspond to methanol (2.21 min) and ethanol (2.66 min), respectively (Fig. 2c). With pure Cu plate as
n 0.2 M PBS solution saturated with Ar (red line) and CO (black line) (For interpretation this article.).
electrode, the faradic efficiencies of methanol and ethanol are 0.8% and 4%, respectively (Fig. 2d). In sharp contrast, the faradic efficiency of methanol on Cu63.9Au36.1 electrode is 15.9%, almost 19 times that for pure Cu. In addition, the faradic efficiency of ethanol is increased to 12%. Pure Cu nanoparticles of similar size were also tested for CO2 reduction, and the corresponding faradic efficiencies of methanol (5.1%) and ethanol (4.6%) are higher than that on bulk Cu but still much lower than that on Cu63.9Au36.1/NCF. Similar pure gold nanoparticles were found not to produce alcohols. These results suggest that Au component in nanostructured CueAu alloy may contribute a lot to enhanced conversion of CO2 to alcohols. To investigate if the nanostructure also affected the catalysis performance, we tested CueAu alloy deposited on smooth copper as working electrode (Fig. 1e) for CO2 reduction. The as-synthesized CueAu alloy is analyzed to be Cu62.6Au37.4, close to that deposited on NCF. However, the faradic efficiencies of methanol and ethanol are only 7.9% and 3.5%, which are much lower than that of Cu63.9Au36.1/NCF. This result indicates that the size and nanostructure of CueAu also affect the conversion efficiencies of alcohols.
Besides alcohols, formate is another major product of CO2 reduction and analysis results are listed in Table 1. The faradic efficiency of formate on nanostructured Cu was much higher than that on Cu63.9Au36.1/NCF. To investigate the effect of Cu content on faradic efficiencies of products from CO2 conversion, different Cue Au/NCF samples with similar nanostructure were prepared by adjustment of deposition potential. With a higher atomic percentage of Cu in CueAu alloys, the faradic efficiency of formate increased while that of alcohols decreased. The results in Table 1 indicate that the suitable addition of Au into Cu alloys may facilitate the reduction of CO2 to alcohols while restraining the formation of formate. According to the publications, two-electron reduction of CO2 to formate or CO was more favorable due to low overpotential [13]. As for the formate, it is identified to be a stable end product and much harder to be reduced into other products (e.g. alcohols) [14,15]. Alternatively, CO is believed to be an important intermediate species, which could be further converted to hydrocarbons or methanol [15]. However, the yield of methanol on pure copper electrode is knownmuch lower than that of CO over a wide potential range [16]. If CO reduction was facilitated, there could be a possibility for the enhancement of further conversion to methanol.
To investigate if as-prepared Cu63.9Au36.1/NCF could catalyze conversion of intermediate product e CO, electrochemical behaviors of nanostructured Cu, nanostructured Au and Cu63.9Au36.1/NCF electrodes were tested in solutions saturated with either Ar or CO. Note that the pH values of both the CO-saturated and Ar-saturated solutions were measured to be close, eliminating effects of proton concentrations on the hydrogen evolution. Fig. 3a shows that hydrogen evolution current is obviously suppressed on nanostructured Cu electrode when CO is present owing to the adsorption of CO on the surface [16]. Similar results are also obtained on the nanostructured Au electrode (Fig. 3b). With Cu63.9Au36.1/NCF as electrode, cathodic current is improved in presence of CO at
potentials less than 0.9 V (Fig. 3c), indicating reduction of CO occurs on Cu63.9Au36.1/NCF. Hence it does appear likely that the alloys facilitate enhanced alcohol production through catalyzing conversion of intermediary CO. Although underlying catalytic mechanism of CueAu alloys is not clear, we expect that results presented here can provide new solution for electrochemical conversion of CO2.

sections.heading: 4. Conclusions
sections.text: Nanostructured CueAu alloys were developed by a templateassisted electrodeposition and showed special catalytic activity towards electrochemical reduction of CO2 to alcohols (methanol or ethanol) in aqueous system. Faradic efficiency of methanol on Cu63.9Au36.1/NCF was analyzed to be 15.9%, which was about 19 times that on pure Cu. In addition, faradic efficiency of ethanol was improved to 12%. Electrochemical analysis showed that CueAu alloys catalyzed not only CO2 reduction, but also CO reduction. The surprisingly multifunctional catalysis of CueAu alloys contributed greatly to the enhanced conversion of CO2 to alcohols. This kind of nanostructured CueAu alloys was believed to be promising catalysts in conversion of CO2 to alcohols.
